title: Tennis elbow and golfer's elbow
intro: Tennis elbow causes pain on the outside of the elbow and golfer's elbow causes pain on the inside. Both are overuse problems of the tendons that attach forearm muscles to the elbow, and you do not need to play either sport to get them. Most cases improve over several months with activity changes and exercise.

sections.heading: Causes
paragraphs: Repetitive gripping, lifting, typing, using tools or racquet sports can overload the tendons at the elbow, leading to small tears and tendon changes. The problem is most common between ages thirty and fifty. Weak forearm muscles, poor technique and sudden increases in activity contribute.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Pain at the bony bump on the outer or inner side of the elbow, spreading down the forearm, that worsens with gripping, lifting a cup, turning a key or shaking hands. The elbow may be tender, and grip can feel weak. Swelling is uncommon. Symptoms can last months, though most people improve by one year.

sections.heading: Self-care
paragraphs: Reduce or modify activities that provoke pain, without stopping all movement. Cool packs after activity can ease soreness, and painkillers or anti-inflammatory gels may help briefly. Adjust grip size and technique, take breaks from repetitive work and use ergonomic tools. A strap worn on the forearm may relieve strain for some people.

sections.heading: Exercise and therapy
paragraphs: Progressive strengthening and stretching of the forearm muscles, ideally guided by a physiotherapist, is the best-supported long-term treatment. Manual therapy and other physical treatments give mixed results. Corticosteroid injections may relieve pain in the short term but are associated with more relapses later, so they are used with caution. Other injections and shock wave therapy have uncertain benefit.

sections.heading: Surgery and outlook
paragraphs: Surgery is rarely needed and is considered only after six to twelve months of failed treatment. Most people recover without it. Prevent recurrence by building forearm strength, using good technique and increasing load gradually.

examples.title: Adapting at work
examples.text: Imagine your elbow hurts after long computer sessions. You could vary your tasks, rest the forearm regularly, adjust mouse and desk height and start strengthening exercises.

examples.title: Choosing treatment
examples.text: Suppose you are offered an injection. You might ask about short-term relief versus later recurrence and whether exercise therapy should come first.
